name: Daria Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I maintain the billing and claims system at a company that sells software to insurance firms. It's an old codebase, fifteen years of layers, and I know which bits you mustn't touch on a Friday. My day is mostly reading tickets from the support team, tracing why a policy got charged twice, and writing a careful fix with tests around it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady and I know it well, and I like the moment a weird bug finally makes sense. What wears me down is the constant push to change how we work: new tools every quarter, and now everyone asking why I don't use the AI assistant. I'm 27, I live with my boyfriend Sam, who's an electrician, and I've saved a good amount, so I'd rather keep things calm than chase the next shiny thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. At work I'd say the old system still needs someone who actually understands it, and the AI tools never did. With friends I'd just be glad the subject goes quiet for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep the job I'm good at, which suits me fine. A bit of routine work getting automated doesn't touch me much, because the hard part of my day is knowing the history of the code. I'd be secure, and that's what I want at this point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep putting money aside, about a thousand a month into the savings account. I'd maybe ask for a pay review, because if the hype dies the people who kept the lights on should get credit. Sam and I would probably finally book the trip to Portugal we keep postponing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Like when a storm forecast turns out to be a bit of rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone asks why you don't use the AI assistant. What do you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell them the truth. I tried the AI assistant once for a billing rule, and it wrote something that looked right and was wrong. That code would have charged ten thousand customers twice. My lead Priya (my team manager) said I was being stubborn. In this picture, I'd feel a bit less stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company has been for sale for a year, so a new owner could still shake things up whatever AI does. That's a background worry, not a big one. With my savings and plenty of other firms in the city, I'd find another job if I had to.

say: The old system still needs someone who **understands it**, and the AI tools never did.
I'd be **glad** the subject finally goes quiet for a while.
think: I keep the **job** I'm good at, which suits me fine.
Knowing the **history of the code** is the hard part, and AI doesn't touch it.
do: Keep saving about **a thousand a month** into the savings account.
Ask for a **pay review** for the people who kept the old system running.
Book the **Portugal trip** with Sam that keeps getting postponed.
feel: **Calm**, like a storm forecast that turns out to be a bit of **rain**.
S0.quote: I tried the AI assistant once for a billing rule, and it wrote something that looked right and was wrong.
fieldNote: One bad experience with the **assistant** shaped her whole view of AI tools.
The only worry left is the **company sale**, which she treats as background noise.
Her **savings** and a busy local job market make her feel secure.

steps.text: Keep fixing billing and claims bugs on the old system
Keep saving about a thousand a month
Ask Priya for a pay review this spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the right things: we'll see where the tools help and keep a human checking the billing. I wouldn't post anything online, I never do. With Sam I'd say it straight, that it looks like my sort of job is the one getting squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be one of the people who gets left behind if I keep refusing the tools. Coding is right there on the list, and my company would love to say one person with AI can do the work of three. I'm average at my job, not a star, so I can't count on being the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd sit tight for a few months and see what the company actually does, because I don't want to jump at shadows. If they start cutting, I'd look at jobs in places that change slowly, like the city council's IT team or a hospital. I'd keep saving and probably skip the Portugal trip for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling-apart anxious, but there's a knot in my stomach when I picture Priya calling a team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Priya did call that meeting, what do you think she'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would say the team is going from eight to five and the five will each have an AI assistant. If my manager Priya calls that team meeting, I'm the only one who's never touched the AI assistant. I wouldn't need anyone to tell me who's first on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you're resistant to the tools, but you also say refusing them puts you on the list. Would you start using them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it came to keeping my job, but I'd hate it. I'd probably learn just enough to show I can, the way you learn a bit of a language before a trip. My heart wouldn't be in it.

Privately to Sam: my sort of job is the one getting **squeezed**.
think: I'll be **left behind** if I keep refusing the tools.
I'm **average**, not a star, so I can't count on being kept.
do: Wait a **few months** to see what the company actually does.
Look at slower-moving employers like the **council IT team** or a hospital.
Skip the **Portugal trip** and keep saving.
feel: **Anxious**, with a knot in her stomach about a **team meeting**.
S1.quote: If my manager Priya calls that team meeting, I'm the only one who's never touched the AI assistant.
fieldNote: Sees clearly that **refusing AI** puts her first on the cut list.
Prefers to **wait and watch** before moving, true to her resistant nature.
Would learn the tools only **grudgingly**, to keep the job.

steps.text: Wait a few months to see the company's plans
Apply to the council IT team if cuts start
Skip the Portugal trip and keep saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say very little in public, because I'd be in shock and I don't like guessing out loud. At work I'd ask management directly what the plan is for the team. To friends I'd say it's moving too fast and nobody's in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of a job within a year or two of it arriving. If AI can do almost any thinking work better and cheaper, then fixing billing code is the easiest thing to hand over. My savings would last a long time, but I'd have nothing to move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away, no holidays, no new car, keep the money in cash. I'd look hard at what Sam does, because electrical work is hands-on and robots don't arrive until about 2031. Maybe I'd ask Sam's boss whether I could train as an apprentice, even though it's a huge change for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake thinking I wasted my twenties learning a job that disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam say if you told him you wanted to train as an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would be kind about it, but Sam would also laugh, because I hate ladders. Sam's always said the trade needs people who read the regulations properly, and I do love a rulebook. It wouldn't be my dream, but it would be three years of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Only three years, though, before robots arrive. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the part I can't think about for long. Maybe by then the government would have to do something, because everyone would be in the same boat. I'm not someone who likes to rely on help, but I'd have to.

say: I'd ask management **directly** what the plan is for the team.
To friends: it's moving **too fast** and nobody's in charge.
think: I'm **out of a job** within a year or two of it arriving.
My savings would last, but I'd have **nothing to move to**.
do: Cut spending at once: **no holidays**, no new car, keep money in cash.
Ask Sam's boss about training as an **electrical apprentice**.
Expect to need **government help** once robots arrive around 2031.
feel: **Alarmed** and lying awake about a **wasted** twenties.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake thinking I wasted my twenties learning a job that disappeared.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose her job** within a year or two of AGI.
Looks to **Sam's trade** for a three-year stopgap before robots.
Uneasy about relying on **help**, but sees no other option later.

steps.text: Cancel holidays and the car purchase, keep savings in cash
Ask Sam's boss about an electrical apprenticeship
Apply for government support if work runs out after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the two-year one, only less panicked: companies and the government have five years to make a plan, so they'd better make one. At work I'd ask for training to be offered to everyone, not just the keen ones. I still wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years just means a slower version of the same end. I'd keep my job for maybe three or four years, and the whole time I'd be watching the team shrink. I don't adapt quickly, so having time doesn't help me as much as it would help someone like Sam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd make myself finally learn the AI assistant properly, because if I'm going to hold on for four years, I need to look useful. I'd save hard, maybe 1,500 a month, so we can buy a small house outright or close to it. Around year three I'd start the electrical course with Sam's help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, just slower. Like watching water rise in a basement when you know there's no pump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you don't adapt quickly. How do you know that about yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When my company moved from one project tool to another, it took me six months to stop hating it, and everyone else took two weeks. I know how I am. I can do new things, but I need time and I need to see they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the AI assistant this time. What changed your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changed my mind about the tools. What changed is that five years is long enough for refusing to look like a choice, not just caution. I'd rather be the person who learned the AI tools late than the person who never did.

say: Companies and government have **five years** to make a plan, so make one.
Offer **training to everyone**, not just the keen colleagues.
think: Five years is a **slower version** of the same end.
I don't adapt quickly, so extra **time** helps me less than it helps Sam.
do: Learn the **AI assistant** properly in the first year to look useful.
Save about **1,500 a month** toward a small house bought nearly outright.
Start an **electrical course** around year three with Sam's help.
feel: **Alarmed** but slower, like water rising in a basement with **no pump**.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the person who learned the AI tools late than the person who never did.
fieldNote: Still expects to **lose the job**, only later, so the mood stays alarmed.
Agrees to learn AI not from conviction but because **refusing** would look like a choice.
Knows her own **pace** of change and plans around it.

steps.text: Learn the AI coding assistant properly in year one
Save about 1,500 a month toward a small house
Start an electrical course around year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. At work I'd say the company should start retraining people now, not in 2034. I'd probably say it more confidently than in the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my developer job ends around 2036, but ten years is long enough for someone slow like me. I'd be 37, which feels young enough to start a second career. I'd have time to try things out properly rather than jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for now and save, and in the next two years I'd do short courses on weekends to find out what I'm actually suited to. I'm thinking building inspection, because it's checking things against rules, and it's on-site work where robots come later. By 2030 I'd want to be fully moved over, with the house mostly paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because I know my job has an end date. But it's a manageable kind of anxious, the kind with a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Building inspection is a big change. What's the pull?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Tom was a building inspector, and Tom used to say the job is reading the rules and then reading the building. That's basically what I do with old code. The difference is the building is real and you have to go there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Sam and you change any plans because of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait a couple of years before having kids, until I know where my second career is going. Sam wants kids sooner, so we'd have to talk about it. I'd rather start a family once I know which job is paying the bills.

say: Ten years is enough time, so there's **no excuse** for being caught out.
The company should start **retraining** people now, not in 2034.
think: My developer job **ends** around 2036, but ten years suits someone slow like me.
At **37**, I'd be young enough to start a second career.
do: Keep the job and do **weekend short courses** over the next two years.
Train toward **building inspection**, on-site work where robots come later.
Aim to have the **house** mostly paid off by 2030.
feel: Still **anxious**, but the manageable kind, **with a calendar**.
S4.quote: My uncle Tom was a building inspector, and Tom used to say the job is reading the rules and then reading the building.
fieldNote: A decade suits her **slow pace**, so this is her least frightening AGI picture.
Links **old-code work** to building inspection through her uncle Tom.
Would **delay children** until her second career is settled, against Sam's wishes.

steps.text: Take weekend short courses to test career options
Delay having children until the new career is settled
Keep saving to pay most of the house off by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without question, because I need time and that picture gives me none. What would help is someone paying for proper retraining with a wage while you do it, so people like me can switch without burning all our savings. Clear dates from the company would help too, so I'm not guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be told you're the problem for not using a tool. Being careful used to be a good thing in software. In some of those pictures, being careful is what gets you fired.

headlineQuote: Being careful used to be a good thing in software. In some of those pictures, being careful is what gets you fired.
portrait: A **27-year-old** developer maintaining an old **billing and claims** system for insurance clients.
Lives with **Sam**, an electrician, and has saved a solid cushion.
Has **never used** AI tools after one bad try, and prefers steady, familiar work.
Calm in the plateau, but **alarmed** in both faster AGI pictures because she adapts slowly.
With a decade, she'd move to **building inspection**, like her uncle Tom.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because she needs time and it gives none.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a wage, so switching doesn't burn her savings.
**Clear dates** from her company, so she isn't guessing.
